content: The raspberry, scientifically classified under the genus Rubus, is an edible fruit that encompasses several species. The term raspberry originally referred specifically to the European species Rubus idaeus, which remains its standard English name in its native regions. Other species closely related to Rubus idaeus within the subgenus Idaeobatus are also referred to as raspberries. These include: Rubus strigosus (commonly known as the American Raspberry, or Rubus idaeus var. strigosus), Rubus arcticus (Arctic Raspberry), Rubus crataegifolius (Korean Raspberry), Rubus occidentalis (Black Raspberry), Rubus odoratus (Flowering Raspberry), Rubus phoenicolasius (Wine Raspberry), Rubus leucodermis (Whitebark or Western Raspberry, also referred to as Blue Raspberry in its native regions). Raspberries are a commercially significant fruit crop cultivated extensively across temperate regions worldwide. Many modern commercial raspberry varieties are hybrids derived from Rubus idaeus and Rubus strigosus. Cultivation Raspberries are grown for both fresh consumption and commercial processing. They are used in products such as individually quick frozen (IQF) fruit, purées, juices, and dried fruit for grocery items. Traditionally, raspberries were a mid-summer crop, but advancements in agricultural technology, breeding, and transportation have enabled year-round availability. Optimal growth requires ample sunlight and water, but excessive moisture or poorly drained soils can lead to Phytophthora root rot, a significant disease affecting red raspberries. Raspberries are relatively easy to cultivate in moist temperate climates but can spread aggressively if not pruned. They often appear as garden weeds due to seed dispersal by birds. Two main types of raspberries are commercially available: summer-bearing varieties, which produce fruit on second-year canes (floricanes) during mid-summer, and ever-bearing varieties, which yield fruit on both first-year canes (primocanes) in late summer and fall, as well as on second-year canes the following summer. Raspberries thrive in USDA hardiness zones 3 to 9. They are traditionally planted as dormant canes during winter, but the use of tender plug plants derived from tissue culture has become increasingly common. A specialized cultivation method known as long cane production involves growing canes for one year in colder climates (e.g., Scotland or Washington State) to meet chilling requirements for budbreak. These canes are then transplanted to warmer regions (e.g., Spain) to produce an early-season crop. Raspberry plants should be spaced approximately one meter apart in fertile, well-drained soil. Raised beds or ridges are often used to mitigate root rot risks. The flowers serve as a significant nectar source for honeybees. Raspberries propagate through basal shoots (suckers) and underground runners, which can lead to invasive growth if not managed. The fruit is harvested when it turns deep red and detaches easily from the receptacle, indicating peak ripeness and sweetness. Excess fruit can be preserved as jam or frozen. Raspberry leaves, which have an astringent flavor, are used in herbal teas and are traditionally believed to regulate menstrual cycles. Each raspberry weighs approximately 4 grams and consists of around 100 drupelets, each containing a juicy pulp and a single seed. Raspberry bushes can yield several pounds of fruit annually. Unlike blackberries, raspberries have a hollow core when removed from the receptacle. Cultivars Numerous raspberry cultivars have been developed, including thornless varieties and those with more upright growth habits that do not require staking. Crossbreeding with black raspberries (Rubus occidentalis) has produced purple raspberries, while hybridization with other Rubus species has resulted in fruits like boysenberries and loganberries. Yellow-fruited cultivars are often referred to as golden raspberries. Nutritional Composition and Potential Health Benefits Raspberries are rich in polyphenol antioxidants, including anthocyanins, which are associated with potential protective effects against various diseases. Their aggregate fruit structure contributes to a high dietary fiber content, making them one of the most fiber-rich plant foods, with up to 20% fiber by total weight. Raspberries are an excellent source of vitamin C (30 mg per cup, providing approximately 50% of the daily value), manganese (60% of the daily value), and dietary fiber (30% of the daily value). They also contain significant amounts of B vitamins (B1, B2, B3), folic acid, magnesium, copper, and iron. Raspberries rank among the top fruits for antioxidant capacity, primarily due to their high levels of ellagic acid (from ellagitannins), quercetin, gallic acid, anthocyanins, cyanidins, pelargonidins, catechins, kaempferol, and salicylic acid. These polyphenolic compounds are under investigation for their potential health benefits. The oxygen radical absorbance capacity (ORAC) of raspberries is approximately 4900 per 100 grams, placing them among the highest-ranking antioxidant fruits. For comparison, cranberries and wild blueberries have ORAC values of around 9000, while apples average 2800. Preliminary research, though not yet confirmed in clinical studies, suggests that regular raspberry consumption may offer protective effects against: Inflammation, Pain, Cancer, Cardiovascular disease, Diabetes, Allergies, Age-related cognitive decline, Degenerative eye conditions associated with aging. Diseases and Pests Raspberry plants are susceptible to damage from the larvae of certain Lepidoptera species (butterflies and moths). For a detailed list, refer to Lepidoptera species that feed on Rubus.
